title: Alcaraz Finds His Rhythm: 'I'm Better Than I Thought' at US Open
summary:
Carlos Alcaraz is sending a warning to the rest of the men's draw: he's back, and he's getting better with every match. The 23-year-old Spaniard swept past China's Wu Yibing 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 on Friday to reach the fourth round of the US Open, continuing his comeback from a wrist injury that sidelined him for 139 days.

"To be honest, I'm better than I thought," said Alcaraz, a seven-time major champion. "Right now, I think my level is really good. I think I have caught the rhythm of the competition. Every time that I step on the court I give it all. I'm just trying to improve, be better every match and I think I'm getting there."

His path to an eighth major title has opened up significantly. World number one Jannik Sinner is absent due to injury, and Novak Djokovic suffered a shock first-round exit to Argentina's Mariano Navone. Canadian third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime also fell early, losing to Karen Khachanov in the second round.

As the second seed, Alcaraz can't meet top-seeded Alexander Zverev until the final. Zverev, the French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up, has looked vulnerable, needing five sets and playing until 2am in both his matches so far.

Alcaraz's next opponent is American 20th seed Tommy Paul, whom he has beaten six times in a row. The only top-10 player he could face before the semifinals is Ben Shelton, who finished his own four-set win over Denis Shapovalov at 2:08am local time. Alcaraz has won all three of their meetings.

A potential semifinal clash with Daniil Medvedev looms, but Alcaraz holds a 6-3 head-to-head advantage, though the Russian beat him at Indian Wells in March.

Alcaraz has won his past 17 matches at Grand Slams, capturing the 2025 US Open and 2026 Australian Open. With his confidence growing and the draw opening up, the defending champion looks increasingly dangerous.
why_it_matters: Time away due to injury is not just personal; when top players miss events, the rankings, prize money, and semifinal spots all shift, which affects the whole sport's hierarchy and the narratives young players follow. Alcaraz returning to form also gives fans a genuine title race rather than a walkover.

background_read: Carlos Alcaraz — the 23-year-old Spanish seven-time major champion — arrived at the US Open (New York's Grand Slam event, played in late summer) as defending champion but had missed 139 days with a wrist injury, an unusually long layoff in a sport that runs year-round.

Tennis has four Grand Slam events — the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and the US Open — all using a single-elimination draw, and 'seeds' are ranking placements meant to keep the strongest players apart in early rounds.

Jannik Sinner (the Italian world No.1) was absent because of injury, while Novak Djokovic (the Serbian player with the most men's Grand Slam titles) lost in the first round to Argentina's Mariano Navone.
With top players dropping out, the remaining section of the draw can open up quickly, but every later match still has to be won against fresh, confident opponents.
Alexander Zverev, the German top seed, is the biggest remaining obstacle until a possible final.

perspectives.description: A fit Alcaraz makes the tournament more exciting, and his attacking game is a box-office draw. Seeing a former champion work his way back after injury can also inspire young players who are dealing with their own setbacks.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / critical — concerns about the tour
perspectives.description: The absent and early-exiting stars raise concern about tennis's physical toll: top players are missing the business end of a major, and matches that end at 2 a.m. are a sign that scheduling and recovery are not going smoothly.

Draws are designed around rankings, not health. When top seeds fall, statistically weaker players suddenly get a clearer path, but that only matters if they handle the pressure of a wide-open section.

If Alcaraz wins another major, the story will be about his quick recovery and the open draw; if he loses early, questions will shift to whether he truly regained match fitness. Either way, the next two rounds will define his season.
